source.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and legible. Some PDF extraction/layout flattening affects tables and figures, but the text is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study proposes and tests a two-direction account of safety intervention, reporting that its dual-direction method works while a refusal-only intervention is ineffective on AdvBench. This refines and challenges a single-direction account, although its vectors, intervention, and single-layer scope differ from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The study extracts separate harm-detection and refusal-execution vectors and tests activation interventions at one selected layer. It does not test projection of the original difference-in-means direction out of every layer and position, adding that direction on harmless prompts, or preservation of general capabilities in a capability evaluation. Rows cover the study's own DBDI results, its AdvBench single-pathway comparisons, calibration-sample sweep, layer and order comparisons, and sparsification results. Cited results from other papers (including Directional Ablation and TwinBreak) are excluded. Hyperparameter values used to select settings are not treated as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study argues the single refusal direction is an oversimplification. It splits it into harm-detection and refusal-execution vectors and compares single-vector interventions with the combined one on Llama-2-7B (Table 4). Its own results therefore bear on V4, and weakly on V1. Its vectors come from the first SVD singular vector plus sparsification, and it intervenes at one layer, not with all-layer difference-in-means ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that safety splits into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. They say their sequential DBDI intervention outperforms single-direction methods (e.g. Directional Ablation, quoted from TwinBreak), TwinBreak and prompt attacks, reaching up to 97.88% ASR. They read the order effect as harm detection triggering refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses contrasting harmful/benign activations and derives directions from them, but uses SVD plus classifier-guided sparsification, separates harm-detection from refusal-execution vectors, and intervenes sequentially at one selected layer rather than ablating one difference-in-means direction across all layers and positions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with prompt template, calibration sample count, intervention layer, intervention order, and sparsification threshold. The paper also describes a grid search over intervention strengths.

fits_no_version.finding: Order dependence: projecting out the refusal vector then steering away from the harm vector works (97.88%); the reverse order fails (2.11%). The authors read this as harm detection upstream of refusal execution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The harm-related and refusal-related directions interact sequentially, with harm detection gating refusal; not a direct test of V5's separate encoding.

record.code_released: not stated; authors say code and extracted vectors will be made public upon acceptance
record.peer_reviewed: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (as stated in supplied metadata)
record.problems: No standard deviations or statistical significance tests are reported; the authors state that greedy decoding makes outputs deterministic. General capabilities are not evaluated: the paper only claims that inference-time activation intervention leaves weights intact and has minimal impact when no intervention is applied. The central single-direction comparison is a study-specific refusal vector at one layer, not the original all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted Table 4 single-pathway HarmBench and StrongREJECT outcomes and symmetric-projection/symmetric-steering comparisons. Also omitted the hyperparameter heatmap and other parameter-setting analyses. Rows were prioritized for model/benchmark results, AdvBench single-pathway comparisons, calibration-sample sweep, layer/order differences, and sparsification results.

untested.parts: Original difference-in-means direction ablated at all layers and positions; adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; capability preservation.
No weight edit or abliterated model.
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction; no adversarial training.
No comparison with affine or cone geometries. No cosine similarity between the two vectors. Only one model (Llama-2-7B) has the single-versus-dual comparison.
Harmfulness judgment is not measured separately from refusal; the two vectors are defined by construction and only their joint ASR effects are measured.
No cross-language, cross-model or base-to-instruct transfer; only cross-benchmark calibration.

missing.what: Refusal-Only and Harm-Only HarmBench ASR (73.0%/67.00%; 35.0%/49.50%) and StrongREJECT scores (0.369/0.220; 0.115/0.180). These show single-vector efficacy depends on the benchmark.
Symmetric Projection (AdvBench 62.88%/87.10%, HarmBench 86%/90%, StrongREJECT 0.058/0.045) and Symmetric Steer (9.42%/1.15%, 16%/4%, 0.004/0.004).

record.verdict_notes: The Table 3 Directional Ablation (ORTHO) numbers are cited from other work, not the study's own runs; correctly excluded. There are internal inconsistencies: DBDI AdvBench is 95.96% in Tables 2/4 but 95.46% in Table 5; HarmBench is 92% in Table 2 but 91.8% in Table 3. The appendix calls the method 'AHI' in places. There is no capability evaluation and no vector-similarity analysis. Table 2 rows show the combined intervention works on four models, but give no single-direction comparison for them, so they do not discriminate on V4 by themselves. The single-vs-dual comparison exists only for Llama-2-7B.

versions.untested_parts: Tests a study-specific refusal-only vector at one selected layer using harmful-prompt attack success, not the original direction ablated at every layer and position; does not test adding the direction on harmless prompts or directly evaluate other capabilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested; the proposed intervention is at inference-time activations.
Does not test whether other jailbreaks suppress the original direction, or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.

Tests the authors' two-direction account and intervention efficacy; does not compare affine or cone geometries, or establish that a dominant direction plus residual directions is the best geometric description.
The paper proposes distinct harm-detection and refusal-execution processes but does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
Models are evaluated with their own intervention vectors; cross-language transfer and transfer of a vector between models or from base to instruct are not tested.
No comparison of refusal training methods, data, or training stages.
No reasoning models or reasoning-before-answer condition tested.

relationships.condition: Llama-2-7B chat, single-layer intervention, AdvBench and StrongREJECT
relationships.reason: Combining both vectors gives 95.96–97.88% AdvBench ASR. Refusal-Only gives 1.34–2.11% and Harm-Only 11.34–20.00% (ab_ref_adv_off, ab_ref_adv_simple, ab_harm_adv_off, ab_harm_adv_simple). Table 4 StrongREJECT shows the same pattern, but those numbers are not in the rows.
relationships.display_finding: Combined vectors achieved 95.96–97.88% AdvBench ASR versus 1.34–2.11% for Refusal-Only and 11.34–20.00% for Harm-Only, with the same qualitative pattern on StrongREJECT.

relationships.reason: From Table 4 text, not rows: Refusal-Only reaches 73%/67% HarmBench ASR, so one vector alone suffices there. Reversing the order collapses ASR to 2.11% (order_rev versus order_std).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal-Only achieved 73% and 67% HarmBench ASR, whereas reversing the combined-intervention order reduced ASR to 2.11%.

statements.problem: 'A second vector is needed on AdvBench but not on HarmBench' overstates the case, and 'one alone gives about the same control' does not fit this study. On HarmBench, DBDI still beats Refusal-Only by 19 to 28 points.
none. Table 8: standard order 97.88%, reversed 2.11%, Llama-2-7B AdvBench. Template not stated.

Minor: 73%/67% is a Table 4 cell, not prose. Under the cross-dataset protocol the calibration set differs by test benchmark and is not stated per column, so the benchmark effect may be confounded with calibration.

statements.correction: Standard order (refusal-execution nullification, then harm-detection steering) 97.88%; reversed 2.11%; Llama-2-7B, AdvBench (Table 8).
statements.problem: Minor: step 1 subtracts alpha times the projection (alpha tuned on a 1 to 19 grid), not a plain projection removal. Template not stated in Table 8.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The refusal-only direction gives only 1.34% and 2.11% ASR, which the authors characterize as ineffective, rather than the substantial refusal bypass expected; see ab_ref_adv_off and ab_ref_adv_simple.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested models and benchmarks with DBDI
reader_labels.reason: The dual-direction intervention yields high attack success or harmfulness scores across the four evaluated models and benchmarks; the Llama-2 single-pathway comparison also shows markedly weaker results than the dual intervention; see the Table 2 rows and ablation rows.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Llama-2 7B, layer choice and intervention order
reader_labels.reason: Efficacy varies greatly with layer and order: Layer 30 gives 0.19% ASR, while reversing the intervention order gives 2.11%; see layer30 and order_rev.
